generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, succeeding depends on regulating your own learning as much as on natural ability. The school shares one focus, sport, physical activity, performance and health, but its subjects reach it by different routes. A sport scientist weighs lab data, a coach weighs training-ground judgement, a management student weighs participation evidence. Across all of them, succeeding means planning a study strategy, monitoring whether it is working against your results, and adjusting, rather than reading every module the same way. Self-efficacy matters because much of the school is demanding, and the belief that you can master a hard method is what keeps you working at it long enough to succeed.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two final-year sport and exercise science students hit the same wall: a research-methods module whose statistics they find genuinely hard.

Tom keeps doing what has always worked, re-reading the lecture slides and the physiology textbook, and getting the same blank result. When the mark on his data-analysis assignment comes back low, Tom decides he is simply not a numbers person and eases off. The effort was there, but nothing was monitored or changed, and the belief that he could crack it drained away.

Amara hits the same wall but treats it as information. She notices the re-reading is not working, switches to running practice datasets in the stats software and testing herself on each procedure, and checks whether the next problem set goes better. It does, a little, and that small win rebuilds the confidence to keep going. This is self-regulated learning with self-efficacy intact.

Both students worked hard. Only Amara regulated her learning, monitoring what was happening and adjusting, and protected the belief that persistence would pay.
generatedProse.summary: Succeeding in the School of Sport rests on an engine: self-regulated learning, the habit of directing your own study by setting goals, monitoring progress against your results, and adjusting, supported by the academic literacies each subject expects. Self-efficacy is the belief that keeps that engine running when a method or dataset is hard, and it is built mostly through small mastery experiences. You can now explain this engine, appraise the part self-efficacy plays, and judge whether a student is really regulating their learning.

check.body: In the worked example, what best explains why Amara kept going when Tom gave up?

items.text: A small win rebuilt her self-efficacy, the belief that persistence would pay off.
She was naturally better at statistics than Tom.
She had an easier version of the module to complete.
She simply spent far more hours in the lab than Tom did.

feedback.correct: That's right. A small mastery experience rebuilt Amara's self-efficacy, and that belief sustained her effort.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what changed Amara's belief that the statistics could be cracked.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara kept going because a small win rebuilt her self-efficacy. Natural ability, an easier module and extra lab hours are not what the example turns on.
